title: Data retention & PII controls demo - Aurora Payments
summary: Redwood AE/SE walked Aurora Payments through the Console and API toggles for request storage, PII redaction, retention windows, KMS integration and audit logging. Customer emphasized PCI constraints and right-to-be-forgotten needs. Agreed next steps: send SOC2 and data protection docs, schedule a security deep-dive and pilot runbook.
topics: Per-route storage toggles and dev/test separation
Optimize recommendations for cost vs. logging

transcript:
Header:
Date: 2025-03-10 | Start: 15:00 PST | Duration: 45 minutes
Attendees: Liam Chen (Redwood AE), Maya Patel (Redwood SE), Rajiv Kapoor (Aurora Head of Platform), Sofia Martinez (Aurora Security), Tom Reynolds (Aurora ML)

[00:00:02] Liam Chen: Hey everyone, thanks for joining, appreciate you making the time. I'm Liam, AE on the Redwood team, and Maya here is our SE who will walk through the Console and the data retention controls.

[00:00:12] Maya Patel: Hi all, quickly: we'll focus today's demo on request storage toggles, PII redaction, retention windows, and integrations like KMS and audit exports. If you want us to dive deeper into any section call it out.

[00:00:25] Rajiv Kapoor: Thanks, quick context — Aurora is a payments processor, we need strict controls around PAN and cardholder data, PCI scope. We're evaluating how Redwood can ensure we don't persist sensitive request data while still getting logs and metrics.

[00:00:40] Sofia Martinez: Also need ability to demonstrate data deletion for audits and support a right-to-be-forgotten workflow, so deletion, export, and legal hold are important.

[00:00:52] Liam Chen: Totally — that's exactly what we'll show. Quick housekeeping: call's being recorded. We'll point to the security docs and SOC2 report and share the pilot runbook after.

[00:01:05] Maya Patel: Jumping into the Console — you'll see the top-level privacy tab. First control is "Request Storage". Default for hosted customers is ON but you can toggle to OFF at the tenant level. We also support per-route overrides so you can keep storage off for card-processing endpoints while keeping it on for non-sensitive routes.

[00:01:30] [screen share noises]

[00:01:33] Maya Patel: Here is the toggle, "Store request payloads" — on/off. When OFF, the runtime drops full request bodies before persisting them to our logs and metrics store. We still emit aggregated metrics like token counts and latencies.

[00:01:49] Tom Reynolds: So when it's off we still get latency histograms and cost numbers?

[00:01:52] Maya Patel: Yes — anonymized metrics remain. We intentionally separate telemetry from payloads. You still get per-request success/failure codes and timing, but payload, metadata headers and raw text are omitted unless you opt in.

[00:02:08] Sofia Martinez: How about partial retention — e.g., redacting PAN but keeping masked versions?

[00:02:12] Maya Patel: Good question. We have a "Redaction Rules" engine. You can apply preset patterns — credit card, SSNs, emails — or add custom regexes. The console shows a preview on sample payloads so you can validate redaction before enabling. Redaction can be configured to: mask, replace with token, or remove field entirely.

[00:02:33] [short pause]

[00:02:35] Liam Chen: To add, for high-security customers we recommend per-route off + redaction at ingress in your stack and also enable BYOK — bring-your-own-key — so encrypted backups and logs are bound to your KMS.

[00:02:50] Rajiv Kapoor: BYOK is critical. We run keys in our KMS. Do you support AWS KMS and HSMs?

[00:02:56] Maya Patel: Yes, we support AWS KMS, GCP KMS, and HSM integrations. Keys are used for at-rest encryption and for encrypting any exported archives. We can provide role-based access so the Redwood ops team cannot decrypt customer-backed stores.

[00:03:12] Sofia Martinez: Is there proof you can't decrypt? Is that in the SOC2 docs?

[00:03:15] Liam Chen: SOC2 covers access controls and key management practices; for BYOK we also provide a key usage audit trail and can work with your security team to run a dual-control process for key rotation. We'll attach the SOC2 and our BYOK integration guide in the follow-up.

[00:03:30] Maya Patel: Next: retention windows — configurable tenant-level setting: 0 (no retention), 30, 90, 365 days, or custom. Important nuance: '0' means no request payloads are persisted; we keep aggregated metrics for 90 days by default unless you opt to change that.

[00:03:47] Tom Reynolds: If we set 30 days and then a POI request comes in, can we flag it for legal hold beyond the window?

[00:03:51] Maya Patel: Yes, we have a 'legal hold' feature. You can tag specific request IDs to be excluded from purge. Legal hold requires an authorised admin action and is logged in the audit trail. We also expose an export API to pull those requests into your long-term archive if needed.

[00:04:07] [keyboard clacking sounds]

[00:04:10] Rajiv Kapoor: We need a right-to-be-forgotten flow from user request to deletion. How fast is deletion propagated across systems?

[00:04:14] Maya Patel: Deletions are near real-time for persisted payloads; the purge job runs continuously and we can provide a confirmed deletion event via webhook to your endpoint. For caches and backups we document retention TTLs and can assist with a one-time purge in the pilot.

[00:04:29] Sofia Martinez: Can we get an SLA for deletion in an enterprise contract?

[00:04:32] Liam Chen: For Dedicated or Private deployments we can contract stricter SLAs and put deletion propagation windows in the agreement. For hosted customers we publish typical windows and we can add contractual terms for enterprise tiers.

[00:04:45] Maya Patel: Now showing the API side — we have a header flag you can set per-call: "X-Redwood-Store: false" which tells the runtime not to persist that request regardless of tenant-level default. Useful for client-side decisioning.

[00:05:00] Tom Reynolds: Nice — so an app gateway could set that header for card flows. Is that header authenticated so a client can't just set it to bypass logging?

[00:05:05] Maya Patel: It's honored only if the request is signed with your tenant's API key and your tenant policy allows header-based overrides. We also log who toggled it and by which key, so auditability is preserved.

[00:05:18] [short laughter]

[00:05:20] Sofia Martinez: One risk is developer error — someone accidentally enabling storage for test endpoints. Do you have guards?

[00:05:24] Maya Patel: Yes, we support route-level policies and protected routes. You can mark routes as "restricted" so only a small set of admins can change retention or storage settings. There's an approval workflow and we surface config drift alerts in the Console.

[00:05:38] Rajiv Kapoor: On logging — we still need stack traces and model debug info for production incidents. How do you provide that without payloads?

[00:05:44] Maya Patel: We separate debug metadata from full payloads. We can capture hashed request fingerprints, tokenized representations, and deterministic anonymized traces. For severe incidents you can opt-in to short-term debug captures (e.g., 72 hours) that require additional RBAC approval and an audit entry.

[00:06:02] Tom Reynolds: What's the workflow for capturing one-off debug traces?

[00:06:05] Liam Chen: Typically a developer opens a ticket, an admin approves a temporary capture window via the Console, and we generate a time-limited export that your team can pull. Everything is logged in the audit trail.

[00:06:16] [screen transition sound]

[00:06:20] Maya Patel: Next I want to show how Optimize ties into this. While Optimize is primarily for cost/performance suggestions (batching, caching, quantization), we also surface recommendations related to data handling: suggest which routes to disable request storage on based on PII detection heuristics and sampling of traffic patterns.

[00:06:36] Rajiv Kapoor: So Optimize will propose turning off storage for endpoints that look like payment or token exchanges?

[00:06:39] Maya Patel: Exactly — it'll score routes by PII-risk and cost tradeoffs. You can accept suggestions or run them in a sandbox before applying. Suggestions come with expected token cost savings and estimated impact on quality metrics.

[00:06:52] Sofia Martinez: How accurate is the PII detection? We can't rely on a false negative for PAN.

[00:06:56] Maya Patel: We provide out-of-the-box high-sensitivity credit-card detectors and allow you to ship in custom patterns. For PAN we recommend a defense-in-depth: ingress-side validation + Redwood redaction + header-level opt-outs.

[00:07:10] Tom Reynolds: If we wanted full control, would Redwood Private solve everything?

[00:07:13] Liam Chen: Private (VPC/on-prem) gives you the most control: private control plane, network isolation, and you hold keys. Many customers with PCI/regulated workloads choose Private or Dedicated hardware so they can define retention behavior and who administers the environment.

[00:07:26] Rajiv Kapoor: Cost tradeoff question: if we disable retention for most routes, do we lose observability that will make debugging costly?

[00:07:31] Maya Patel: You trade some raw telemetry for privacy. Our recommendation is a hybrid pattern: keep aggregated metrics on, enable short-term debug captures with RBAC for a handful of routes, and persist non-sensitive routes fully. Optimize will simulate and estimate observability loss vs cost savings.

[00:07:46] [15 second pause while Maya pulls up a sample payload]

[00:08:02] Maya Patel: Demo: sample payload containing card number, email, shipping address. I'll apply the card-number regex redaction rule. Preview shows the PAN masked to **** **** **** 1234. You can toggle mask vs remove.

[00:08:18] Sofia Martinez: Can we canonicalize masked format so our client logs match?

[00:08:21] Maya Patel: Yes — you can define replacement templates. Also we support tokenization: replace PAN with a canonical token that maps to hashed fingerprint you control.

[00:08:32] Tom Reynolds: For auditability we need to link masked logs to transaction IDs. Does Redwood preserve correlation IDs when redaction is applied?

[00:08:37] Maya Patel: Yes correlation IDs are retained unless explicitly set to be redacted. You can configure which headers are considered sensitive.

[00:08:46] Rajiv Kapoor: About exports — we want nightly export to our S3 for long-term retention. Is that supported?

[00:08:50] Maya Patel: We support scheduled exports (S3, GCS) and streaming webhooks. Exports can be encrypted with your KMS key. For hosted customers we can set up a secure connector; for Private it's direct.

[00:09:02] Sofia Martinez: Who has access to those exports on Redwood side?

[00:09:05] Liam Chen: Access is restricted to your tenant admins. By default Redwood ops does not have access to customer exports; with BYOK and restricted export permissions you control key rotation and access. We'll include the exact access table in the docs.

[00:09:18] [crosstalk]

[00:09:22] Maya Patel: Now quick note on audit logs: every admin action (change retention window, redaction rule, legal hold) is recorded with actor, timestamp, and IP. Audit logs are immutable and downloadable.

[00:09:34] Rajiv Kapoor: We'll need those for auditors. Can we have automated alerts if someone changes retention for a protected route?

[00:09:38] Maya Patel: Yes — alerting hooks for config changes. You can route alerts to Slack, PagerDuty, or an internal webhook.

[00:09:46] Tom Reynolds: How about integration with our SIEM?

[00:09:49] Maya Patel: We provide a stream of audit events to SIEMs and a native Splunk/Datadog connector. Events include admin actions, export events, and deletion confirmations.

[00:09:59] [brief pause]

[00:10:05] Liam Chen: I'd like to surface a couple of real customer patterns: one payment customer uses per-route off + masked tokenization + daily S3 export for reconciliations; another uses Private deployment to keep logs entirely inside their network and only allow exports mediated by their key.

[00:10:22] Rajiv Kapoor: For the audit we might need raw logs for a subset of users under legal order. How quick can Redwood rehydrate?

[00:10:28] Maya Patel: If you opted to archive to your S3, rehydration is immediate. If requests were never persisted (tenant-level OFF and no export), then there's nothing to rehydrate. For the legal hold flow, we recommend tagging before purge so those records are retained in your archive.

[00:10:42] Sofia Martinez: Ok, let's talk about the pilot. We want to test with two endpoints: tokenization flow and refunds. We'll need to simulate production traffic and run redaction rules.

[00:10:50] Liam Chen: Great. Our typical pilot plan: 2-4 week sandbox, sampling traffic, apply retention rules, run Optimize suggestions, measure observability impact. We'll share the runbook.

[00:11:00] Tom Reynolds: Any blockers on our side for the pilot?

[00:11:03] Maya Patel: We'll need sample payloads, a whitelist of routes, and a contact for security review so we can provision BYOK and restricted roles.

[00:11:10] Rajiv Kapoor: We'll supply that. A legal question: how do you handle subpoenas for hosted customers?

[00:11:14] Liam Chen: We respond to legal process per our terms; for hosted customers we will produce data we have access to, and customers with BYOK/Private are able to control and produce their own archives. We'll share the legal FAQ in the follow-up.

[00:11:27] Sofia Martinez: Can we get a network diagram for hosted vs private?

[00:11:30] Maya Patel: Yes — we'll attach architecture diagrams: hosted with Redwood-managed network, Dedicated with customer VPC peering, and Private with on-prem.

[00:11:39] [sounds of note taking]

[00:11:44] Liam Chen: I'll recap quickly: we'll share SOC2 and data protection docs; Maya will schedule a security deep dive; Aurora to share sample payloads and route list; we'll send pilot runbook and proposed pricing for retention tiers.

[00:11:57] Rajiv Kapoor: Sounds good. One last thing — can we get an example contract clause for deletion SLAs?

[00:12:03] Liam Chen: Yes, we'll include sample contract language. For Dedicated/Private we can add stricter deletion SLA clauses.

[00:12:10] Sofia Martinez: Thanks, that covers most of it.

[00:12:13] Liam Chen: Great — thanks all, we'll follow up with the docs and next steps.

[00:12:18] [meeting closed — remaining time used for one-on-one follow-up]

Notes on transcription: occasional mis-heard words around acronyms (KMSs -> KSM), names slightly off in auto-transcribe (Rajesh -> Rajiv) and timestamps approximate.
